A catalog is a JSON Schema document describing components, functions and Markdown instructions; the agent streams `createSurface`/`updateComponents`/`updateDataModel`/`deleteSurface` as a flat adjacency list with `@path`/`@call` bindings, and the human's clicks come back as `action` events with a resolved context, plus v1.0 bidirectional RPC (`callRendererFunction`, `callAgentFunction`) with `allowedCallers` (`rendererOnly`/`agentOnly`/`rendererOrAgent`) and `requiresUserActivation` enforcement — the agent cannot ship arbitrary code or invoke a local-only function ([spec](https://a2ui.org/specification/v1.0-a2ui/), [messages](https://a2ui.org/concepts/messages/)). Three SDK layers (Core/Agent/Renderer) mean server-side validation and client-side message resolution share one implementation per language, and official renderers exist for React, Lit, Angular, Flutter, SwiftUI and Jetpack Compose with accessibility attributes mapped onto WAI-ARIA, Flutter Semantics and iOS/Android accessibility APIs ([SDK matrix](https://a2ui.org/concepts/sdks/)). Adoption is real: AndroidX publishes `androidx.a2ui:a2ui-engine`/`a2ui-model` for a native Compose renderer, Flutter ships a GenUI layer, and CopilotKit renders A2UI natively ([Jetpack release notes](https://developer.android.com/jetpack/androidx/releases/a2ui), [CopilotKit A2UI](https://docs.copilotkit.ai/generative-ui/a2ui), [Flutter GenUI](https://docs.flutter.dev/ai/genui)). The honest objections: it has no visual design language of its own (v1.0 deliberately removed `theme` so branding is the host app's job), a custom component still needs an implementation per native platform until the roadmap's "primitives you style to your design system and describe once" lands, the Dart Agent SDK has no skill generation yet, and the AndroidX artifacts are still `1.0.0-alpha02`. Those gaps are addressed by shipping your own catalog per platform (styled with Material 3/SwiftUI/shadcn), pinning protocol v1.0 and running the conformance suites, and using the TypeScript or Python Agent SDK for skill generation ([roadmap](https://a2ui.org/roadmap/), [ecosystem](https://a2ui.org/ecosystem/renderers/)).

**json-render** — The runner-up and the most complete generative-UI *toolkit*: `defineCatalog` with Zod-typed props and actions, `defineRegistry`, a flat `{root, elements}` spec, expressions (`$state`, `$cond`, `$template`, `$computed`), `visible` conditions, watchers, streaming compilation, `catalog.prompt()` for system prompts, a spec-tree/state-editor/action-log devtools panel, 36 pre-built shadcn components, and per-package agent skills for Cursor/Claude Code/Codex ([README](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render), [skills](https://json-render.dev/docs/skills), [renderers](https://json-render.dev/docs/renderers)). It also reaches outputs no UI toolkit covers — PDF, email, Remotion video, terminal Ink, chat cards, SVG/PNG. What keeps it second: "native" means React Native only, with no SwiftUI, Compose or Flutter renderer, and its A2UI support is a documentation page explicitly labelled illustrative, showing the older `surfaceUpdate`/`beginRendering` message shapes rather than v1.0 envelopes ([A2UI page](https://json-render.dev/docs/a2ui)). If your agents need to emit documents, video and terminal screens more than true native mobile, this becomes the better pick.

**CopilotKit** — The best agent *runtime* of the set: `CopilotRuntime` v2 with AG-UI streaming, `createCopilotRuntimeHandler`, `useAgent`, shared state, human-in-the-loop, and surfaces for React, Angular, Vue, React Native, Slack and Teams. It is also the clearest evidence that A2UI is winning: its generative-UI page documents A2UI as one of three modes with `a2ui: {}` on the runtime and a renderer that activates with no frontend code ([A2UI docs](https://docs.copilotkit.ai/generative-ui/a2ui)). The trade-off: it is an agent application stack, not a cross-platform design system — React-first, React Native support is experimental and needs crypto/polyfill setup, and there is no native iOS/Android widget renderer. If the agent runtime and transport matter more than the pixel layer, choose CopilotKit and put A2UI underneath it.

**Fluent UI** — The most enterprise-proven React design language: `@fluentui/react-components` is a converged package (the result of deduping `@fluentui/react` and `@fluentui/react-northstar`), and theming is a `FluentProvider` with a theme object at the root of the app ([react-components README](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui/blob/master/packages/react-components/react-components/README.md)). It is a genuinely good human-facing system for Microsoft 365-class products, but it is React/web only and ships no agent-authored UI path: no catalog, no protocol, no runtime surface an agent can emit into. The irony is that Microsoft's own ecosystem already supplies that path — CopilotKit and MCP Apps both live there — so a Fluent team can adopt A2UI or MCP Apps without leaving the org, but nothing in this repo does it yet, and the "across web and native" half of the brief is unaddressed.

**MCP Apps** — The transport-and-trust standard for agent UI: tools declare `ui://` resources, hosts render them in a sandboxed iframe with explicit CSP (`connectDomains`, `resourceDomains`, `frameDomains`, `baseUriDomains`), optional camera/microphone/geolocation/clipboard permissions, `prefersBorder`, and bidirectional JSON-RPC through the host ([README](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps), [spec](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps/blob/main/specification/2026-01-26/apps.mdx)). It ships four agent skills so coding agents can scaffold apps. But it is HTML in an iframe — no native widgets, no design language of its own, and the repo ships no supported host implementation (hosts are tracked in a client matrix). A2UI's `McpApp` component embeds these inside A2UI surfaces, which is how I'd use it: MCP Apps for the sandbox, A2UI for the native surface.

**Ouro UI** — The most explicitly "people and agents" *branding* in the list: Ouro HX for screens a person uses, Ouro AX for the interfaces an agent uses (CLI, HTTP API, MCP server), with an `ax-claims` standard, an `ax-xray` conformance checker that calls your interface the way an agent would, and a `ouro-check` skill running axe-core, overlap, clipped-text and jank checks ([README](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui)). The trade-off is structural: the two halves are *different surfaces for different audiences* rather than one interface both use; the Apple Swift package is not yet 1.0 stable; Android and Windows are unbuilt; and everything except the AX kit is React web. Best pick if your "agents" are CLI/API consumers rather than authors of UI.

**Agent-native (Builder.io)** — The cleanest "one declaration, two audiences" model: `defineAction()` produces a single source of truth consumed by the React UI, the agent, HTTP, MCP, A2A and a CLI, with typed outcomes and wait cursors ([README](https://github.com/BuilderIO/agent-native)). It is also the honest answer for "the agent drives the same screen a person uses" without a UI protocol at all. But it is web-only (React + Nitro + PostgreSQL) and cannot satisfy "across web and native" by itself.

**Material 3 and Jetpack Compose** — The strongest native human-facing system: M3 color/typography/shape tokens via `MaterialTheme`, dynamic color, M3 Expressive ([M3 docs](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/designsystems/material3)). Critically for this brief, Google now ships a Compose A2UI renderer in AndroidX that parses and schema-validates A2UI messages and renders native Compose components "without executing arbitrary code" ([Jetpack A2UI](https://developer.android.com/jetpack/androidx/releases/a2ui)). So the agent story exists — but only through A2UI, the artifacts are alpha, and you still have to author the catalog that carries M3 styling. Pair M3 with A2UI rather than choosing it alone.

**Flutter** — Renders natively on web, iOS, Android, desktop and embedded, from one codebase, and ships a GenUI SDK that composes UI from a JSON catalog of your Flutter widgets and feeds state back to the agent as a "high-bandwidth loop" ([GenUI docs](https://docs.flutter.dev/ai/genui)). Google's own framing is "Flutter + A2UI = GenUI" from I/O 2026, and A2UI lists `a2ui_flutter` as an official renderer. Objections: the GenUI package is alpha, and its JSON is Flutter-specific rather than a portable protocol, so an agent written for Flutter can't also target iOS-native or Android-native clients.

**SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines** — The reference for native human quality on Apple platforms: SwiftUI's own documentation and the HIG are the source of truth for how a screen should behave and look, and the A2UI project ships an official `A2UISwiftUI` renderer package precisely so agent-authored surfaces land as real SwiftUI views rather than screenshots or HTML ([SwiftUI docs](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui), [A2UI SDK matrix](https://a2ui.org/concepts/sdks/)). Standalone, however, it offers nothing for agents: an agent can only write Swift code, with no protocol, no catalog, no guardrail layer, no native/web parity, and no way to stream a partial interface. That objection is answered by using HIG as the design authority and A2UI as the contract — SwiftUI is the Apple-side rendering target inside the winning protocol, not the agent-facing system on its own.

**shadcn/ui** — The best-known "agents can build with this" story: copy-own registry components plus AI Elements, the official agentic pattern layer built on `Trace` so every agent step (Reasoning, Tool, Plan, Queue, Subagent, Confirmation, Terminal, Sources) has one shape ([AI Elements](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/ai-elements)). But it is React/Next/Tailwind-only, patterns are components you copy, and nothing lets an agent emit *runtime* UI to a native app — the agent is a code author, not a UI author.

**Tamagui** — Real web + React Native parity from one TypeScript component tree, with an optimizing compiler that flattens styles into atomic CSS. Its agent story is codegen assistance (`npx tamagui generate-prompt`, installable skills), not agent-authored runtime UI, and its "native" is React Native rather than Swift/Kotlin widgets ([docs](https://tamagui.dev/docs/intro/introduction)). Strong pick for a React-native app that wants one UI codebase; not a fit when an agent must drive real native surfaces.

**React Aria and React Spectrum** — The accessibility and internationalization benchmark: 50+ unstyled accessible components, 30+ locales, 13 calendars, RTL, a documented screen-reader interaction matrix, plus hooks/components that work in React and React Native ([react-aria](https://react-aria.adobe.com/)). For agents it is a well-documented API surface to write code against, with no protocol, no catalog and no runtime agent-authored UI. Pair it with a generator, not as the generator.

**Base UI** — MUI's unstyled primitives with a modern headless API, and unusually agent-friendly *docs*: every page has a "View as Markdown" link and the handbook ships `llms.txt` ([quick start](https://base-ui.com/react/overview/quick-start)). That makes it an excellent target for agents that write code — and, via the community A2UI ecosystem, it underpins Ouro UI's registry items. But it is React/web only, and "LLM-friendly docs" is not "agents that author running UI".

**Radix UI** — Low-level, WAI-ARIA-correct unstyled primitives: the best substrate if you want deterministic behavior and a known API surface for agent-generated code. Nothing agent-specific ships, it is React/web only, and there is no native story at all ([primitives](https://github.com/radix-ui/primitives)). Its role in any agentic design is as the accessible layer beneath shadcn-style registries.

**MUI** — A large, mature, themeable React library with design kits and CSS utilities, and it is what many A2UI community renderers target (a community renderer inherits the host `ThemeProvider` and adds validation checks and streaming placeholders). One concrete caveat from MUI's own page: "Material UI currently adopts Material Design 2" — so if you need M3 fidelity, Compose or the M3 Expressive React renderer are better ([MUI](https://mui.com/material-ui/)). React/web only; no first-party agent-authored UI path.

**Chakra UI** — Accessible React component system (MIT, v3 on Ark) with a consistent API and documented focus styling, good for shipping human-facing web quickly ([repo](https://github.com/chakra-ui/chakra-ui)). For agents it is a code-generation target only: no protocol, no catalog, no runtime path, and no native. If your agent story is "the agent writes your React components," Chakra works; if it is "the agent composes the screen," it doesn't.

**OpenAI Apps SDK UI** — A real design system with tokens and Radix-based React components for ChatGPT apps, paired with an MCP-based delivery path ([repo](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui)). The ceiling is the problem: it targets one host, ChatGPT, has no native target, and provides no mechanism for an agent to author UI at runtime — you'd reach for MCP Apps or A2UI for that.

**Vercel UI SDK** — A beta behaviors library (`@ui-sdk/core` with React/Vue/Svelte/Solid/Web Components adapters) and one of the few docs sets that explicitly include "Build with an Agent", "Connect an Agent" and WebMCP sections ([docs](https://ui-sdk.dev/docs)). But beta, web-only, no native renderer, and the "agent" sections are integration recipes rather than a component contract — too early to bet a cross-platform design system on.

**AI Elements** — Vercel's agentic component patterns, notable for being superseded: the repository's own README states the package is deprecated with end of life in November 2026 in favor of shadcn/ui's version ([repo](https://github.com/vercel/ai-elements)). The patterns (Agent, Tool, Reason, Plan, Subagent) are still a good catalogue of what an agent-facing UI needs, and shadcn/ui's AI Elements is where you should actually build — but don't adopt the Vercel package itself, and note both are React/web, with no native.
actions.pullQuote: A2UI turns agent-generated UI into validated data, with official renderers for React, Flutter, SwiftUI and Compose.
actions.testimonial: I chose A2UI because it treats generated UI as validated data instead of code: catalogs are JSON Schema contracts, functions carry allowedCallers and requiresUserActivation rules, and callRendererFunction/callAgentFunction give agents and people two-way control over the same surface. The renderer SDKs for React, Lit, Angular, Flutter, SwiftUI and Jetpack Compose mean one agent-authored interface lands as native widgets rather than a WebView, and the spec maps accessibility attributes onto each host's real a11y APIs. The honest trade-off versus json-render, which I passed on, is that A2UI has no visual design language of its own — I would have to author a catalog per platform and implement custom components natively until the roadmap's declarative primitives ship. I still picked it because the catalog contract, stateful validation and per-platform accessibility mapping are the parts that keep a generative interface trustworthy in front of a real user.
